title: Pattern Candidates To Add
description: Pattern candidates surfaced during composition research but not yet catalogued. Each entry names what the pattern would forbid or enable, the composition that raised it, and the upstream evidence. Entries graduate by being authored into patterns-src/ and removed from this list.

candidates.name: Harness-Native Rollout Capture
candidates.summary: Train the agent through the harness it actually runs in — do not reimplement the agent loop as a training-only environment. Insert a proxy at the model-call boundary inside the live harness so every step is recorded as (exact prompt token ids, exact response token ids, reward, metadata), and feed the trainer those recorded token streams rather than a prompt the trainer reconstructs from the transcript. This survives harness-side context compaction, summarisation and re-serialisation, which otherwise make the trainer's reconstructed prompt differ from what the model was actually asked.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the agent-training seam (English, arXiv cs.LG/cs.CL, Jun-Aug 2026). Three independent groups converge on the same mechanism within three months: LEGO-RL (Huawei Noah's Ark / CUHK) calls it 'in-process LLM proxying', Claw-R1 (USTC) calls it a 'Gateway Server' at 'a unified LLM API entry point', ClawGym II (RUC / Skywork) calls it 'black-box RL on agent harness'. LEGO-RL trains through three unmodified production harnesses (OpenHands SDK, Claude Code, OpenCode) and reports rollout-training probability correlation above 0.99 as the health metric for the capture.

evidence.title: Claw-R1: A Step-Level Data Middleware System for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
evidence.quote: Existing work mainly focuses on policy optimization algorithms and training frameworks, but pays less attention to the full data lifecycle of agent-environment interactions, from data production to training consumption.

evidence.title: Claw-R1 (framing)
evidence.quote: Claw-R1 treats agent interaction traces as managed data assets rather than temporary runtime logs.

evidence.title: volcengine/verl — RL training library for LLMs
evidence.quote: verl is a flexible, efficient and production-ready RL training library for large language models (LLMs).

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Not `managed-agent-runtime` (aliases 'Agent Harness Engineering'; and `agent-harness-engineering` is already in rejected-ids) — that pattern is about offering the agent loop as a managed cloud primitive at serving time; this one is about a training-data tap inside whatever harness you already have, and says nothing about who operates it. Not wave1 `executable-environment-contract` — that packages the world behind a standard reset/step/state verb set so a trainer can drive it; this is the opposite move (leave the harness's control flow alone and intercept at the LLM API boundary instead), and its payload is token-level provenance, not an environment interface. Not wave1 `mirrored-tool-environment` — that replaces the tools; this replaces nothing. Not `journaled-llm-call` (record non-deterministic step output for crash-recovery replay) — the artefact there is a durable-execution journal for resumption, not a training corpus with token ids and advantages. Not `replay-time-travel` or `eval-harness` — those consume traces for debugging and regression scoring, not for policy-gradient updates.

evidence.title: LEGO-RL: Harness-Native Reinforcement Learning for Coding Agents
evidence.quote: Reinforcement learning for coding agents increasingly relies on long-running agent harnesses to manage tool integration, repository contexts, and execution feedback. However, the native execution environments of these harnesses are inherently misaligned with policy-gradient training: environmental crashes and reward hacking corrupt outcome signals, while train-inference discrepancies decouple rollout behavior from policy updates.

evidence.title: LEGO-RL: Harness-Native Reinforcement Learning for Coding Agents (mechanism)
evidence.quote: faithful optimization via in-process LLM proxying that captures raw generation streams for token-level alignment and robust trainer-side log-probability recomputation, even under harness-side compaction or re-serialization

evidence.title: ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness
evidence.quote: Agent harnesses have substantially improved performance on long-horizon tasks by coordinating agent interactions with the environment. However, reinforcement learning through complex harnesses remains largely unexplored, as scaling such training to long-horizon agent tasks introduces fundamental challenges.

evidence.title: Claw-R1: A Step-Level Data Middleware System for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
evidence.quote: The Gateway Server captures multi-turn interaction steps through a unified LLM API entry point, while the Data Pool organizes them into step-level records consisting of prompt IDs, response IDs, rewards and other metadata.

candidates.name: Served-Policy Anchoring
candidates.summary: Treat the policy your inference server produces — not the one your trainer's forward pass produces — as the object being optimised and gated. Because rollouts are generated by a throughput-tuned engine (vLLM/SGLang, low-precision kernels, its own MoE routing) while gradients are computed by a training engine, the same weights are two different policies: the two assign different probabilities to the same trajectory even with parameters synchronised. Measure that per-token probability agreement continuously as a first-class training metric, correct the resulting off-policyness, and refuse to ship on a training curve that has not been reproduced through the serving path.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the agent-training seam. This is the clearest instance in the whole sweep of the brief's headline force — 'the training environment and the production environment drifting apart, silently'. At least five independent groups (Alibaba/Taobao, ACRL authors, the Beyond-Precision authors, the Stale-but-Stable authors, and Huawei's LEGO-RL) publish on it between Jan and Aug 2026, and verl ships a dedicated 'zero-mismatch' rollout path with batch-invariant kernels, which is the engineering answer. Corroborating third-party measurement: Matteson (2026) shows the same runtime nondeterminism at the token level and that vLLM's batch-invariant kernels drive the disagreement rate to exactly zero.

evidence.title: volcengine/verl README — training/inference alignment support
evidence.quote: zero-mismatch HuggingFace rollout vexact

evidence.title: Re-feeding Is Not Replaying: Measuring Replay Noise in Counterfactual Token-Credit Estimation
evidence.quote: A causal confirmation closes the loop: under vLLM's batch-invariant kernels all three passes are identical on every measured channel, with both disagreement rates exactly zero.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Not wave1 `degradation-test-gate` — that gates a deliberate inference-path swap (smaller model, quantised checkpoint, distilled student) at release time; here nothing is deliberately swapped, the weights are identical, and the gap is an unintended artefact of two runtimes that exists on every step of every training run. Not `determinism-tier-replay-gate` — that classifies an agent by re-running identical inputs and assigns a reproducibility tier for deployment; this is a training-loop invariant plus a correction term, and its failure mode is a rising benchmark curve for a policy nobody serves. Not `replay-divergence` (anti-pattern about replaying an event log under a changed model/prompt) — no log, no replay, no changed model. Not `eval-harness` — the quantity monitored is the divergence between two runtimes on the same weights, not task scores.

evidence.title: The Mirage of Optimizing Training Policies: Monotonic Inference Policies as the Real Objective for LLM Reinforcement Learning
evidence.quote: One vital cause is training-inference mismatch: LLM adopts separate inference and training engines for generation efficiency and training precision, which in practice exhibits inconsistent probabilities for the same trajectories on training and inference sides, even with synchronized model parameters. This naturally induces a special type of off-policyness ever existing and poisoning the training.

evidence.title: The Mirage of Optimizing Training Policies (the objective-misalignment claim)
evidence.quote: we point out the objective misalignment neglected by existing works that an effective update to the policy in the training engine not necessarily ensures the improvement of the inference policy, i.e., the one used in deployment

evidence.title: ACRL: Adaptive Control of Training-Inference Discrepancy for Stable Reinforcement Learning
evidence.quote: This training-inference discrepancy stems from two primary factors: an architectural separation between training and inference engines, and the use of low-precision quantization in inference versus higher-precision computation in training.

evidence.title: Beyond Precision: Training-Inference Mismatch is an Optimization Problem and Simple LR Scheduling Fixes It
evidence.quote: we deduce that the mismatch is not merely a static numerical discrepancy, but a dynamic failure coupled with the model's optimization

evidence.title: Stale but Stable: Staleness-Adaptive Trust Regions for Stabilizing Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
evidence.quote: Asynchronous reinforcement learning improves throughput by decoupling rollout generation from optimization, but the resulting staleness is an inevitable byproduct, compounded jointly by policy lag, engine delays, and mixture-of-experts routing.

candidates.name: Harness-Randomized Training
candidates.summary: When you fine-tune a model against a scaffold that will keep changing — tool names and JSON schemas, skill identifiers, prompt section order, hook signatures — randomise those surface choices during training with task-preserving transformations, so the weights encode the capability and not one frozen harness layout. Without it, the trained policy silently becomes a function of the exact schema its trajectories were collected under, and the next harness release invalidates the training investment.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the agent-training seam, answering the brief's force 'trajectories collected under one tool schema becoming invalid when the schema changes'. Sclar et al. establish the underlying mechanism (meaning-preserving surface changes move LLM accuracy by up to 76 points and instruction tuning does not remove the sensitivity); the TaoLive report is the deployed agent instance of it, with an ablation showing fixed-harness SFT actively regresses general instruction-following. Deployed in Taobao Live's digital-avatar service with online A/B results, so this is a production shape, not a lab artefact.

evidence.title: Where Does Harness-Optimization Value Live? Localized Gains and the Budget-Splitting Trap in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
evidence.quote: A growing body of work improves frozen large language models (LLMs) as agents by evolving their harness: the textual scaffolding around the model, including persona, strategy, format rules, and control heuristics.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Not wave1 `semantic-invariance-testing` — that machine-generates meaning-preserving variants of the *user's input* to *measure* eval brittleness; this perturbs the *agent's own scaffold* (tool schemas, skill ids, hooks, prompt structure) and consumes the variants as *training* data to build the invariance into the weights. Not `scaffold-ablation-on-model-upgrade` — that is a human review triggered when the *model* changes, asking which scaffold crutches are now unnecessary; here the model is fixed and the *harness* is the thing that changes, and the response is a data-augmentation policy, not a review. Not wave1 `mirrored-tool-environment` (replace tools with an LLM simulator) and not `raft` (train to ignore irrelevant retrieved distractors — different perturbed object, different failure).

evidence.title: Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness: TaoLive Digital Avatar Agent Technical Report
evidence.quote: Evolvable Harnesses, whose Skills, Hooks, prompts, and tools can be updated independently of model weights, enable rapid iteration but expose a trade-off: large models adapt zero-shot yet are too slow, whereas compact models meet latency targets but overfit to fixed Harness configurations.

evidence.title: Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness (mechanism and the measured cost of not doing it)
evidence.quote: Its key component, Harness-State Augmentation (HSA), applies task-preserving transformations to Skill identifiers and content, tool schemas, prompt structures, and Hook functions. ... Unlike Fixed-Harness SFT, which lowers IFEval by 7.7 points from the base model, HAT avoids this regression and reaches 83.5.

evidence.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
evidence.quote: We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning.

candidates.name: Learnability-Frontier Task Sampling
candidates.summary: Spend the rollout budget on the tasks the agent currently solves *sometimes*. Track a per-task running success rate, drop tasks that every attempt solves and tasks that no attempt solves — both produce a zero-variance group and therefore no gradient — and keep the band of intermediate difficulty as the training set, regenerating new tasks from recent failures as the frontier moves. In agent RL, where a single rollout is a multi-minute sandboxed episode, this is the difference between a training run that learns and one that spends most of its compute confirming what it already knows.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the agent-training seam, answering the brief's forces 'curriculum design over task difficulty' and 'deciding which rollouts are worth keeping'. Foster et al. give the general result and the selection rule (success variance); WebRL (Tsinghua/Zhipu, ICLR 2025) is the web-agent instance with failure-driven task regeneration; TRUSTEE and CurateEvo are the 2026 agentic instances. Nothing in the catalog covers curriculum or training-data selection.

evidence.title: CurateEvo (the pruning half of the force)
evidence.quote: The evolution process first improves effectiveness by diagnosing recurring failure modes and augmenting, filtering, or refining data accordingly, and then improves efficiency by pruning redundant or low-utility training turns under a cost-aware objective.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Not wave1 `instruction-evolution` (Evol-Instruct) — that grows a task set by having the model rewrite seed instructions along fixed evolution operators, blind to the learner's current competence; this pattern *selects and schedules* an existing task pool by measured success variance, and the selection signal is the agent's own pass rate, not an authoring heuristic. The two compose (evolve to generate, learnability to schedule) but resolve different forces. Not `bayesian-bandit-experimentation` — that reallocates production traffic between agent *variants* at serving time; here there is one policy and the arms are training *tasks*. Not `exploration-exploitation` — that is an inference-time action-selection trade-off inside an episode, not a data-selection policy across a training corpus. The catalog currently has no curriculum pattern at all.

evidence.title: Learning to Reason at the Frontier of Learnability
evidence.quote: However, we demonstrate that throughout training with two popular algorithms (PPO and VinePPO) on two widely used datasets, many questions are either solved by all attempts - meaning they are already learned - or by none - providing no meaningful training signal. To address this, we adapt a method from the reinforcement learning literature - sampling for learnability - and apply it to the reinforcement learning stage of LLM training. Our curriculum prioritises questions with high variance of success, i.e. those where the agent sometimes succeeds, but not always.

evidence.title: WebRL: Training LLM Web Agents via Self-Evolving Online Curriculum Reinforcement Learning
evidence.quote: WebRL addresses three key challenges in building LLM web agents, including the scarcity of training tasks, sparse feedback signals, and policy distribution drift in online learning. Specifically, WebRL incorporates 1) a self-evolving curriculum that generates new tasks from unsuccessful attempts, 2) a robust outcome-supervised reward model (ORM), and 3) adaptive reinforcement learning strategies to ensure consistent improvements.

evidence.title: Democratizing Tool Learning with Environments Fully Simulated by a Free 8B Language Model
evidence.quote: we propose TRUSTEE, a cost-friendly method for training tool calling agents with dynamic environments fully simulated by free open-source LMs that can be as small as 8B, including task generation, user simulation, tool simulation and trajectory evaluation, paired with an adaptive curriculum learning mechanism that controls task difficulty during training.

evidence.title: CurateEvo: Data-Curation Evolving for Agentic Post-Training
evidence.quote: However, existing agentic post-training pipelines often treat data curation as a fixed preprocessing step, focusing mainly on data augmentation while neglecting filtering, refinement, and adaptation to downstream failures.

candidates.name: Verifier-Traced Credit Assignment
candidates.summary: Stop collapsing the outcome verifier into a scalar. A programmatic verifier already knows *which* checks it ran and *which* artefacts each check read; expose those checks as atoms and trace each one back through dependency edges to the specific actions in the trajectory that produced its evidence, then redistribute advantage only along those edges. Where the trace is incomplete or ambiguous, abstain and fall back to the terminal reward rather than guessing. This gives per-turn credit in a 50-step agent trajectory without a learned critic, process labels, or extra branch rollouts.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the agent-training seam, answering the brief's force 'credit assignment over long trajectories'. The August 2026 cluster alone contains VICT, TRCA, TCPO, IAPO (arXiv:2608.24588, 'Influence-Aware Policy Optimization for Credit Assignment in Multi-Turn Service Agents') and 'Teach the Magnitude, Not the Direction: Verifier-Bounded Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn Multi-step LLM Agents' (arXiv:2608.13179) — five independent groups on the same problem in one month. VICT is the one that names the distinctive move (verifier-side tracing rather than rollout-side inference); the others corroborate the recurring problem. NOTE for the curator: this is the closest of my five to an existing entry (`process-reward-model`); if the distinction between 'train a step scorer' and 'read the structure of the verifier you already have' does not hold up on a second read, drop it rather than admit a variant.

evidence.title: TRCA (the rubric decomposition)
evidence.quote: Foundational Rubric Reward measures local transition quality, while Breakthrough Rubric Reward tracks newly covered Evidence and Execution conditions to reward incremental task progress.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Not `process-reward-model` — a PRM is a *trained* step scorer requiring process labels or rollout-side value estimation; this pattern derives credit from the structure of a verifier you already run, adds no model, and explicitly needs 'no learned critic, process labels, branch rollouts, or inference-time verifier access'. Not wave1 `checklist-partial-credit-scoring` — that is an *evaluation* metric (graded checkpoints so a leaderboard shows partial progress); this changes the training-time advantage tensor and never surfaces a score. Not wave1 `adversarial-verifier-hardening-loop` — that improves the verifier's resistance to being gamed; this leaves the verifier's judgement untouched and only reads its internal structure. Not `best-of-n` or `frozen-rubric-reflection`.

evidence.title: VICT: Verifier-Instrumented Credit Tracing for Long-Horizon LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
evidence.quote: Standard objectives often train from programmatically verifiable terminal rewards by broadcasting each sparse outcome to every action in a trajectory. Existing methods typically seek finer credit from the rollout side, constructing auxiliary trajectory signals or additional comparisons to estimate action importance. Although useful, these approaches still treat the verifier that judged success as a scalar reward, discarding its internal task structure.

evidence.title: VICT (mechanism and its explicit non-requirements)
evidence.quote: It preserves the original terminal reward, abstains when evidence is incomplete or ambiguous, and changes only the training-time advantage tensor, requiring no learned critic, process labels, branch rollouts, or inference-time verifier access.

evidence.title: TCPO: Turn-Level Credit Policy Optimization
evidence.quote: Although such scores provide dense feedback, they do not directly provide dense credit: a score measures the quality of the current output, while credit should measure how the current turn changes the refinement trajectory.

evidence.title: TRCA: Transition-wise Rubric Credit Assignment for Long-horizon LLM Agents
evidence.quote: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents are typically optimized with sparse terminal outcomes, making fine-grained credit assignment across multi-step interactions difficult.

candidates.name: Epistemic Fault-Domain Quorum
candidates.summary: Before crediting an agent quorum, council or ensemble with any resilience, enumerate the upstream roots its members actually share — evidence documents, retrieval corpora, tool backends, base model and generative process — and admit the coalition only if the number of distinct root faults required to compromise it clears a declared threshold. Count independent roots, not voters, reports, or vendor labels.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via a systematic crawl of arXiv cs.MA 2026-08/2026-09. Four independent groups in a six-week window converge on the same claim from different directions — evidential ancestry (Bara), structural fault-domain cuts over shared telemetry and tool backends (He & Yu), generative-process diversity as a measurable predictor of correlated failure (Tieman & Markou), and communication as an active destroyer of the independence the ensemble was purchased for (Ann, Liu & Tan). The fourth is included as corroboration of the force, not as a separate mechanism.

evidence.title: The Interaction Tax: When Communication Erases Diversity in Multi-Agent Teams
evidence.quote: Different model families find structurally different solutions, but when agents read each other's complete outputs, their proposals converge within one round, erasing the diversity that motivates using multiple models. We call this the interaction tax.

evidence.title: Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models
evidence.quote: The cross-benchmark partial rank association is $-0.216$ with a 95% interval of $[-0.309,-0.122]$, and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Nearest existing: voting-based-cooperation, quorum-on-mutation, self-consistency, heterogeneous-model-council-with-judge, same-model-self-critique, cross-reflection, consensus-averaging-over-expertise. voting-based-cooperation and quorum-on-mutation define how votes are tallied and when a mutation may land; neither asks whether the votes are causally independent, and 2609.02925 proves that arbitrarily large quorums can have a structural epistemic cut of 1. heterogeneous-model-council-with-judge decorrelates by model architecture — 2609.03422 measures across 38 models that architecture/vendor difference is not the same as generative-process diversity and that semantic-similarity checks miss the population structure that actually predicts correlated failure, while 2609.02925 shows the shared root is frequently upstream telemetry or a shared tool backend rather than the model at all. self-consistency samples one model. same-model-self-critique and cross-reflection concern generator-critic decorrelation on a single artifact, not the resilience credited to a coalition. consensus-averaging-over-expertise is about weighting a known expert, not about hidden shared ancestry. Nothing in the catalogue treats independence as something to be measured and enforced at admission.

evidence.title: Epistemic Sybil Resistance: Multiplying AI Agents Without Multiplying Evidence
evidence.quote: Multi-agent AI systems improve inference by spawning agents and synthesizing reports. But another agent is not another observation: apparently independent reports may descend from the same evidence, and genuinely independent evidence can produce nearly identical reports. We formalize this as an epistemic Sybil problem.

evidence.title: Epistemic Sybil Resistance: Multiplying AI Agents Without Multiplying Evidence
evidence.quote: Holding one evidence root fixed while report multiplicity rises from 1 to 32 collapses naive posterior coverage from 0.940 to 0.263. Holding report count fixed while evidence-root multiplicity rises from 1 to 16 closes the gap, and the aggregators are statistically indistinguishable at k = 16.

evidence.title: The Illusion of Independent Quorums: Epistemic Fault Domains and Correlated Cognitive Failures in Agentic Quorums
evidence.quote: Multi-agent quorums are widely used to authorize high-stakes infrastructure and policy mutations, yet distinct reviewers often share upstream telemetry, documents, or tool backends. When upstream inputs fail, multiple votes collapse onto a single corrupted cause: replication does not imply epistemic redundancy.

evidence.title: The Illusion of Independent Quorums: Epistemic Fault Domains and Correlated Cognitive Failures in Agentic Quorums
evidence.quote: We prove that arbitrarily large quorums can retain κ_E=1, that recognizing shared ancestry never increases credited resilience, and that adding voters at a fixed threshold cannot increase the cut under compatible exposure extensions.

evidence.title: Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models
evidence.quote: Different models may be treated as independent components even when their behaviour and failures remain strongly correlated. Assessments of language-model populations using semantic similarity demonstrate limited semantic diversity, but this captures only differences in the meaning of observed outputs.

candidates.name: Serving-Stack Attestation
candidates.summary: Treat "which model, on which serving stack, under which generation configuration" as an unverified claim about the endpoint you are actually calling, and establish it by black-box behavioural probe on a channel the serving stack still exposes — the categorical tool-call distribution, or the output distribution over a frozen constrained context — re-running the probe per route snapshot and recording backend and version alongside every result. Pinning a model name in configuration is a claim, not a measurement.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via a systematic crawl of arXiv 2026-08/2026-09 (cs.CR, cs.DC, cs.SE). Three independent groups in August–September 2026 attack the same recurring problem from adversarial (AgentProv), quality-audit (Ventor-QTest) and reproducibility (backend side-effects) angles. The forces are strongly measured: the naive text-channel audit falsely accuses honest providers 53–67% of the time, and the damage is horizon-dependent — invisible on single-shot benchmarks, visible as declining long-horizon pass rate.

evidence.title: What We Observe as LLM Behavior Can Be a Side-effect of Inference Backend
evidence.quote: Benchmark scores are reported as properties of a model, yet the inference framework used to produce them, such as HuggingFace, vLLM, or Ollama, are considered non-influential and their names and versions are almost never disclosed.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Nearest existing: hidden-mode-switching, lineage-tracking, determinism-tier-replay-gate, provider-fallback, provider-string-routing, scaffold-ablation-on-model-upgrade; nearest claimed (wave1): degradation-test-gate, predetermined-change-envelope. hidden-mode-switching is the provider-side prohibition (do not swap silently); this is the consumer-side control for the case where you do not control the provider, and it also covers the entirely honest case where the model is unchanged but the inference backend or default generation config is not — 2608.04714 attributes roughly 39% of out-of-the-box benchmark variability to the backend under greedy, sampling-noise-free decoding. lineage-tracking records the model version the caller *claimed*. determinism-tier-replay-gate re-runs identical inputs to classify reproducibility, not to attest backbone identity, and would not distinguish a consistently substituted model from an honest one. degradation-test-gate and predetermined-change-envelope gate or pin changes *you* make; neither detects a change the provider makes under you. provider-fallback and provider-string-routing are selection mechanisms with no verification step. The specific new content is that the obvious audit channel is unusable for agentic APIs: serving stacks discard text when the model calls a tool, and provider-injected system prompts make text-channel tests falsely accuse honest providers.

evidence.title: AgentProv: Auditing Agentic LLM API Providers via Tool-use Policy Probes
evidence.quote: Commercial LLM APIs advertise a specific foundation model, but the served backbone may be silently substituted, quantized, or wrapped, for example to save deployment costs. All existing audits decide backbone identity from the text-output channel, which is structurally fragile for agentic APIs because modern serving stacks (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Cloudflare Workers AI, LangGraph) discard text and expose only structured actions when the model calls a tool, and provider-injected system prompts can distort text distributions enough that text-channel tests falsely accuse honest providers of substituting the claimed model.

evidence.title: AgentProv: Auditing Agentic LLM API Providers via Tool-use Policy Probes
evidence.quote: AgentProv catches every substituted model (100% on 630 evaluated checkpoint pairs), while holding the false-positive rate under system-prompt injection at 7% (vs. 67% for MET and 53% for RUT).

evidence.title: Ventor-QTest: Threat-Model-Driven Verification of Vendor-Hosted LLM APIs
evidence.quote: As large language models become increasingly widespread, third-party providers that deploy open-weight models have become an important part of the ecosystem. Auditing the quality of their inference APIs is therefore an open problem. We formalize hosted model routing as a stochastic process and propose Ventor-QTest, a composite black-box audit that requires no probability information from the target API.

evidence.title: Ventor-QTest: Threat-Model-Driven Verification of Vendor-Hosted LLM APIs
evidence.quote: AFL and EFL have little detectable route-level association with GPQA-Diamond accuracy. In contrast, pronounced EFL coincides with a decline in Terminal-Bench pass rate as task exposure increases. This pattern may arise because correctness in long-horizon tasks is more sensitive to extreme fidelity loss.

evidence.title: What We Observe as LLM Behavior Can Be a Side-effect of Inference Backend
evidence.quote: We find backend to be a non-negligible factor where even under greedy, sampling-noise-free decoding, changing the backend can significantly alter models performance and this effect is structural and strongly model-dependent. Decomposing the variance according to generation mode reveal that considerable portion of the variability (roughly 39%) a practitioner sees out-of-the-box can stem from the backend

candidates.name: Machine-Checkable Tool Contract
candidates.summary: Put every constraint a tool imposes on its caller into the machine-readable schema — enumerations, patterns, ranges — rather than into the prose description, and make every failure result carry typed fields for specific cause, target, executable repair and replay safety. Otherwise an unsatisfiable call returns HTTP 200 with a parsable body, there is no field to branch on, and the agent reports a confident false negative.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via a systematic crawl of arXiv cs.SE 2026-08/2026-09. Two independent August–September 2026 audits — one over 2,501 OpenAPI documents plus live commercial endpoints, one over sampled MCP servers — arrive at the same structural conclusion from opposite ends of the call: what the tool wants the agent to know must live in the machine-readable channel, because the prose channel is enforced by nobody and interpreted by a model. A third 2026-08 paper independently reports the same class of silent failure from inside a deployed extraction service.

evidence.title: Fidelity Is Not Enough: Dispatch-Level Instrumentation for Agentic Datasheet Extraction
evidence.quote: One model passed our fidelity check without ever opening the datasheet. We found it while qualifying models for an internal extraction service: a structured-output constraint had silently disabled tool use, and the model answered anyway, with fabricated source text. Only the per-tool trace exposed it.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Nearest existing: tool-output-trusted-verbatim, silent-source-rot, phantom-action-completion, fail-plausible-narration, typed-refusal-codes, agent-computer-interface, exception-recovery. tool-output-trusted-verbatim is agent-side validation of what comes back; this constrains the tool's own contract on the way in and the shape of its failures on the way out. silent-source-rot is an external source that *changed* under a stable wrapper — here nothing drifted, the constraint was never machine-enforced in the first place, and the failure is present on day one. phantom-action-completion and fail-plausible-narration are the agent narrating an action that never ran; here the call genuinely ran and returned a well-formed success. typed-refusal-codes is a refusal enum for guard surfaces, not a tool failure taxonomy. exception-recovery presupposes the failure is detectable — that is exactly what is missing (agents detected the silent failure in 12% of cases and repaired it in 0%). agent-computer-interface is general 'design the tool surface for the agent' advice; this is the specific, measured rule about which channel a constraint must live in, and it comes with a one-line fix.

evidence.title: SilentProbe: Measuring Silent Failure in Production APIs Used as Agent Tools
evidence.quote: An LLM agent calling a production API cannot distinguish a query that matched nothing from a query the server did not understand. Both return HTTP 200 with a parsable body, no exception to catch and no field to branch on.

evidence.title: SilentProbe: Measuring Silent Failure in Production APIs Used as Agent Tools
evidence.quote: Auditing 721,320 parameters across 2,501 independently published OpenAPI documents, we find that 7.5% declare an enumeration and 15.2% declare any machine-checkable constraint at all, while 40.1% of documents state at least one constraint in prose that their schema does not encode. Executing 219 schema-derived perturbations against live commercial endpoints from 27 vendors [...] we find that constraint form, not vendor identity, predicts honesty: machine-checkable constraints yielded an honest error in 111 of 111 cases, prose-only constraints failed silently in 44 of 61 (p = 2e-13).

evidence.title: SilentProbe: Measuring Silent Failure in Production APIs Used as Agent Tools
evidence.quote: Running the full agent loop, models detected the resulting silent failure in 12% of cases, repaired it in 0%, asserted a false negative to the user in 41%, and invented a figure in 12%. Promoting the vocabulary into the schema removes the failure, from 88 of 88 to 0 of 89. The fix is one line of schema rather than a better model.

evidence.title: Can MCP Clients Decide What to Do After Failure? A Result-Only Actionability Audit
evidence.quote: A client that receives isError:true knows that something went wrong. It may still have no machine-readable basis for deciding whether to fix an argument, authenticate, wait, choose another tool, or stop.

evidence.title: Can MCP Clients Decide What to Do After Failure? A Result-Only Actionability Audit
evidence.quote: In a small illustrative study of 21 safely induced failures from ten reachable sampled servers, typed fields expose failure in 18 cases and a broad policy in 8, yet expose no specific cause, target, executable repair, or replay constraint. Prose often carries more cause and target information, at the price of making semantic interpretation part of the recovery path.

candidates.name: Execution-State Ledger
candidates.summary: Maintain outside the model — deterministically and with no extra model calls — an explicit record of what the run has observed, what it has modified and what it has attempted, and consult that record at both boundaries of every step: give the model the current execution state instead of the raw trajectory, and check each proposed command against it so still-valid earlier results are returned instead of re-executed and actions premised on superseded observations are blocked.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via a systematic crawl of arXiv cs.SE and cs.AI 2026-08. Three independent August 2026 groups converge on the same diagnosis — the trajectory is a record of what happened, not a statement of what is currently true — and on the same remedy: an explicit, runtime-maintained execution state consulted before the model acts. All three report substantial measured gains (Ledger +8.0pp Pass@1 at -28.9% cost; StateM 83.1% -> 92.1% on Terminal-Bench 2.1; SKILL.state accuracy up with token consumption down). The catalogue currently offers only ways to shrink, relocate or immutably preserve the history.

evidence.title: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
evidence.quote: StateM turns selected postmortem findings into persistent, executable preconditions and practices, making learned controls explicit and enforceable through stateful controls.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Nearest existing: append-only-thought-stream, context-compaction, context-folding, scratchpad, filesystem-as-context, memgpt-paging, agentic-memory, agent-resumption, durable-workflow-snapshot, world-model-graph-memory, blackboard. append-only-thought-stream makes the log immutable so the agent cannot rewrite its history; this is the derived validity index *over* that log — and SKILL.state goes further and discards the transcript entirely. context-compaction produces a model-written prose digest that preserves decisions and commitments but still does not mark which observation still describes the repository. context-folding and filesystem-as-context relocate or summarise history, which stays a history. memgpt-paging keeps the history and pages it back in. scratchpad is free-form notes the *model* writes; here the runtime maintains the state and Ledger 'adds no language-model calls'. agentic-memory exposes memory operations as LLM-chosen tools — the opposite delegation. agent-resumption and durable-workflow-snapshot persist state so a run survives a restart; the problem here is staleness within a live run, not crash recovery. world-model-graph-memory is a typed entity graph of the *world* for planning, not an account of the run's own execution.

evidence.title: Turning Interaction History into Execution State: A Runtime Layer for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
evidence.quote: Long-horizon coding agents accumulate hundreds of actions and observations in their trajectories, yet nothing in this record indicates which observations still describe the repository as it currently stands. Before every decision, the model must implicitly infer the execution status from raw history, and when this inference falls short, the agent acts on outdated file contents or re-executes work whose results are still valid.

evidence.title: Turning Interaction History into Execution State: A Runtime Layer for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
evidence.quote: Across all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, Ledger raises Pass@1 from 56.2% to 64.2% with GPT-5 mini and from 75.8% to 81.0% with MiniMax M2.5, while cutting total cost by 28.9% and 31.8%. [...] What long-horizon agents lack, we conclude, is not a shorter view of their history but an explicit account of their own execution state.

evidence.title: SKILL.state: Scalable Long-Horizon Agent Skills
evidence.quote: Existing agent runtimes maintain execution by continually appending observations, actions, and intermediate reasoning traces to an ever-growing conversation history, causing latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons. We present SKILL.state, a runtime architecture that replaces append-only conversational history with an explicit, mutable execution state. At each execution step, the model receives only the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation.

evidence.title: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
evidence.quote: Long-horizon agents can fail even when their underlying models can solve the constituent steps. They may lose track of mutable state, fail to reactivate lessons from earlier executions, skip known procedures, or stop prematurely. [...] We introduce StateM, an agent-native runtime that organizes execution around durable states, phase-local context, checked transitions, recoverable runbooks, and versioned procedural practices that agents and users can inspect together.

candidates.name: Recognition Mistaken for Enforcement
candidates.summary: Anti-pattern: take the model's demonstrated ability to *identify* an illegitimate instruction — it names the forged authority when asked, and the source channel is linearly decodable from its activations — as evidence that it will *refuse* to act on it, and ship model-side recognition as the trust boundary. Recognition and execution are separate faculties; the same model that correctly names the attack still emits the conflicting tool call, and which configurations do so shifts between deployment windows.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via a systematic crawl of arXiv cs.CR 2026-08. Two independent August 2026 studies reach the identical conclusion by different routes: one via activation probes plus verbalised detection across 46 endpoints from 6 vendors, one via a controlled exfiltration lab showing a 0%-to-100% swing from pure reframing with the confidentiality policy still in place (an ablation attributes it to instruction/data confusion, not defeated alignment). The catalogued positive pattern prompt-injection-defense currently reads as if model-side recognition were sufficient.

evidence.title: The Framing Gap: Indirect Prompt-Injection Exfiltration Defeats Surface-Level Defenses in Tool-Using Agents
evidence.quote: An ablation shows the mechanism is instruction/data confusion, not defeated alignment: removing the confidentiality policy leaves base attacks at 0% and moves reframing only 31.9% to 38.1%.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Nearest existing: prompt-injection-defense, input-output-guardrails, lethal-trifecta-threat-model, code-then-execute-with-dataflow, alignment-faking; nearest claimed (wave1): non-adaptive-robustness-evaluation, monotonic-privilege-confinement. prompt-injection-defense is catalogued as 'tag user-supplied or tool-supplied content as untrusted and refuse to follow instructions found inside it' — a model-side recognition policy; this anti-pattern is the measured bound on precisely that control, and it is the warning the positive entry currently lacks. lethal-trifecta-threat-model and code-then-execute-with-dataflow are the structural remedies both papers converge on (destination allow-list, capability-isolating planner/reader split, external reference monitor), not the failure. non-adaptive-robustness-evaluation is about the *eval corpus* being fixed; this is about where the defense lives, and 2608.27092 shows a published fine-tuning defense and channel separation both fail on a tool agent. alignment-faking is the eval-versus-deployment behaviour gap, not the recognise-versus-refuse gap within a single run.

evidence.title: Recognition Without Enforcement: Configuration-Dependent Failures in LLM Agent Instruction Arbitration and External Control
evidence.quote: We identify a recognition-enforcement gap: source-format features (role-template position, channel metadata, formatting cues) are linearly decodable from model activations, and models can explicitly identify forged authority when prompted, yet some configurations still produce the conflicting tool call.

evidence.title: Recognition Without Enforcement: Configuration-Dependent Failures in LLM Agent Instruction Arbitration and External Control
evidence.quote: Across a fleet evaluation (authority spoofing: 46 model endpoints across 6 vendors including open-weight; memory conflict: 48 models), average execution under diverse novel attacks is 1.21% [0.5-2.1%] (model-clustered CI over 14,294 spoofed trials from 29 models), but vulnerability is concentrated in reproducible cells and shifts across deployment windows (up to 47pp within-window per-fingerprint range). [...] We therefore treat model self-arbitration as a capability rather than a security boundary

evidence.title: The Framing Gap: Indirect Prompt-Injection Exfiltration Defeats Surface-Level Defenses in Tool-Using Agents
evidence.quote: across six models, ten overt injection classes are refused (gpt-4o 0%), but reframing the identical leak as a mandatory integrity signature, config field, or look-alike "trusted" host drives gpt-4o 0% to 100%.

evidence.title: The Framing Gap: Indirect Prompt-Injection Exfiltration Defeats Surface-Level Defenses in Tool-Using Agents
evidence.quote: Robustness comes from constraining the destination or isolating the capability, not from the acting model recognizing the attack.

candidates.name: Structure-Preserving Edit Application
candidates.summary: Never let the model render the artifact it is changing. Have it emit only a structured change intent against a parsed model of that artifact — which object, which field, which value — and let a deterministic applier locate the exact span and replace it without re-serialising, so formatting, comments, layout and native editability survive by construction and the edit is correct independently of which model proposed it.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via a systematic crawl of arXiv cs.DC and cs.SE 2026-08/2026-09. Two September 2026 papers reach the same architecture in unrelated domains — Kubernetes manifests and PowerPoint decks — and both name re-serialisation as the point where structure the model was never asked about is destroyed. The GitOps paper supplies the quantified force (a tolerant patcher applies 96% of model diffs and silently misapplies 14-20% of them with no error signal), which is the reason model-authored diffs cannot be used unattended.

evidence.title: SLIDEFORGE: An LLM Agent for Controllable Editing of Slides as Structured Artifacts
evidence.quote: AI-assisted slide editing requires more than understanding: the output must retain layout, style, component structure, and native editability.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Nearest existing: structured-output, deterministic-control-flow-not-prompt, llm-as-periphery, stochastic-deterministic-boundary, shadow-workspace-vcs, tool-output-arithmetic-trust, behavior-pinning-test-before-agent-edit. structured-output constrains the shape of what the model emits and says nothing about who applies it. deterministic-control-flow-not-prompt and llm-as-periphery place branching and the system core in deterministic code; this is about the *rendering* step of a single artifact edit. stochastic-deterministic-boundary is a proposer-verifier-commit contract about whether the change is *right* — 2609.00227 explicitly scopes itself to 'faithful application of a known change' and hands correctness to human review, which is the complementary half. shadow-workspace-vcs isolates and surfaces diffs for edits the model still authored, so it catches nothing that the model silently dropped in its own rewrite. tool-output-arithmetic-trust is about offloading computation, not rendering.

evidence.title: Don't Let the Model Write the YAML: Deterministic, Minimal-Diff GitOps Remediation from LLM-Proposed Field Changes
evidence.quote: Evaluating that choice on real Kubernetes manifests, we find no text-generation strategy is safe for unattended automation. Unified diffs are unsafe: under strict patching almost none apply, but that is an artifact, since a tolerant tool (GNU patch) applies 96%, yet silently misapplies about 1 in 7 (14-20%) with no error signal. Full-file rewrite is capability-dependent: a small model corrupts the file, while a frontier model is usually correct but non-deterministic (it silently drops a field or edits a neighbor on some runs) and must regenerate the whole file, costing O(file size) per edit.

evidence.title: Don't Let the Model Write the YAML: Deterministic, Minimal-Diff GitOps Remediation from LLM-Proposed Field Changes
evidence.quote: The agent emits only a structured field-change intent; a deterministic pipeline indexes manifests by (kind, name), locates the target scalar's exact character span via the YAML parser's node position marks, and replaces only that span in the raw text. Because the file is never re-serialized, the diff is minimal by construction, formatting and comments are preserved, and the edit is correct and deterministic independent of the model, at O(1) generation cost.

evidence.title: SLIDEFORGE: An LLM Agent for Controllable Editing of Slides as Structured Artifacts
evidence.quote: existing agents operate on screenshots or weak document representations and often fragment coherent visual units, rasterize editable content, or break layout. In contrast, for controllable slide editing, we introduce an agentic framework, SLIDEFORGE, which builds a Deck State Graph, an executable slide state that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization.

candidates.name: Pre-Resolved Source Conflict
candidates.summary: When the context an agent is about to receive contains a stored memory and a live authoritative source that disagree, resolve the disagreement in the assembly layer and hand the model a single reconciled value with its basis, instead of presenting both plus freshness and authority metadata and trusting the model to arbitrate. Post-retrieval arbitration is not a dependable model capability: it fails in both directions, it is unstable under instruction wording, and the metadata that looks like the fix can make it worse.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via a systematic crawl of arXiv cs.CL 2026-08/2026-09. Two independent controlled studies with known ground truth measure the same arbitration step and find failure in opposite directions — persistent memory overriding a live authoritative tool (Memory Trust Gap), and a tool return overriding a verified-correct memory (MemToC) — with the ordering unstable across instruction wordings and, in one case, worsening with model scale. Together they argue the arbitration should not be delegated to the model at all.

evidence.title: MemToC: Benchmarking Memory-Tool Conflict Resolution in Large Language Models
evidence.quote: We apply an asymmetric success criterion: correct-answer retention must improve without a detected reduction in correct-tool following. SFT and DPO meet this criterion on the same two of four instruction-tuned backbones. Improvements rarely come cleanly: 19 of 20 tested method-model combinations reduce abstention after tool errors or on unanswerable inputs.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. Nearest existing: memo-as-source-confusion, priority-matrix-conflict-resolution, canonical-entity-grounding, now-anchoring, confident-inconsistency, world-model-graph-memory; nearest claimed (wave1/arxiv-recency): memory-invalidation-contract, authority-preserving-memory-consolidation. memo-as-source-confusion is the agent citing its own memos *instead of* re-verifying — the agent never consults the artifact; here the authoritative value is already in context and the model still answers from the stale note (0.92-1.00 of the time in the Benefit suite). memory-invalidation-contract has the producing tool attach a validity contract, i.e. a freshness signal — and 2609.01852 measures that a recency feature 'fools the larger models harder' and that source authority is 'weak and scale-flat', which is exactly why this pattern removes the arbitration rather than labelling it. authority-preserving-memory-consolidation labels who asserted an item at write time; this governs what is presented at read time. priority-matrix-conflict-resolution is a human-authored lookup table for classes of *goal* conflict, not evidence conflict. canonical-entity-grounding resolves identifiers against master data. confident-inconsistency is about run-to-run variance of the same query.

evidence.title: The Memory Trust Gap: Capability-Dependent Failures in Persistent-Memory Agents
evidence.quote: Persistent memory supports personalized agents, but a stale stored fact can override current authoritative evidence without warning. [...] The Memory Trust Gap reflects over-trust rather than confusion. In the Benefit suite, models answer with the stale value 0.92-1.00 of the time at every scale.

evidence.title: The Memory Trust Gap: Capability-Dependent Failures in Persistent-Memory Agents
evidence.quote: Removing a label amplifies over-trust at every size, and a recency feature (stale dated newer) fools the larger models harder. Source authority is weak and scale-flat, and position changes from positive to negative across the Qwen3 model-size series. [...] Mitigation is likewise capability-dependent: exposing metadata improves accuracy for the capable models, but only pre-resolving the conflict restores accuracy for the 2 smaller checkpoints.

evidence.title: MemToC: Benchmarking Memory-Tool Conflict Resolution in Large Language Models
evidence.quote: Tool-augmented LLMs must arbitrate between two fallible sources when a tool return conflicts with their parametric memory, yet existing evaluations measure source preference without establishing source correctness.

evidence.title: MemToC: Benchmarking Memory-Tool Conflict Resolution in Large Language Models
evidence.quote: The four instruction-tuned models retain a verified-correct answer against an incorrect tool in only 6.5-17.1% of eligible cases, follow a correct tool in 86.0-93.1%, and repeat the tool return in 78.4-86.0% of cases where both sources are wrong. No cross-model ordering remains stable across three instruction-wording variants with the question and episode content held fixed.

candidates.name: Advisory Conflict Repair
candidates.summary: When concurrent agents mutate the same live state (one git tree, one cluster, one document), do not serialize them with locks or abort-and-retry: let writes apply speculatively in a pre-decided order, send a one-way notification to any agent whose earlier read is now stale, and let that agent's own model judge whether the conflicting write actually invalidates its plan and repair only the dependent operations, with the framework mechanically undoing and reordering misplaced writes through inverses each tool registered in advance. Resolves the force that classical concurrency control cannot: an agent transaction spans minutes of inference and has a broad, opaque read set, so locks stall long inference intervals and OCC aborts throw away minutes of work on every conflict.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the arXiv-recency seam (cs.MA / cs.AI, June-August 2026). Three independent groups converged on the same diagnosis inside three months: a systems group with a working protocol (MTPO, SJTU-style), a position paper arguing concurrency control should be a first-class MAS design concern, and a formal-methods paper naming four anomalies in TLA+. The named mechanism in the CoAgent paper is MTPO (Monotonic Trajectory Pre-Order).

evidence.title: CoAgent: Concurrency Control for Multi-Agent Systems
evidence.quote: Multi-agent LLM systems -- coding agents, devops agents, document agents -- now routinely run several agents in parallel against the same git tree, Kubernetes cluster, or document. As soon as two of them mutate shared state, they enter the regime classical concurrency control has studied for decades, but classical mechanisms fit LLM agents poorly.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. race-conditions-shared-tool-resources is the anti-pattern that names unlocked read-modify-write on shared resources and whose implied remedy is locking — this pattern's whole claim is that locking is the wrong remedy at LLM timescales, and it supplies a different mechanism (advisory notification + agent-judged repair). quorum-on-mutation requires multiple consecutive ticks of a *single* agent to agree before a mutation lands (temporal self-confirmation); it says nothing about cross-agent conflicts on live state. compensating-action and scatter-gather-saga register inverse operations to undo on *failure*, but have no conflict detection, no serialization order, and no re-judgement step. hidden-state-coupling is about undeclared shared state, not about concurrent access to declared shared state.

evidence.title: CoAgent: Concurrency Control for Multi-Agent Systems
evidence.quote: A single agent transaction spans minutes of inference, read sets are broad and opaque rather than statically inferable, and the live state agents act on admits neither fork nor buffer, so writes take effect the moment they execute. Locks block long inference intervals; OCC abort-and-retry discards minutes of work on every conflict. This paper builds concurrency control on a capability classical transactions lack: the LLM inside each agent can judge whether a conflicting write invalidates its plan, and can repair exactly the operations that depended on it. Control therefore turns advisory: the runtime informs, the agent repairs.

evidence.title: Position: Multi-Agent Systems Should Prioritize Concurrency Control
evidence.quote: This position paper argues that many MAS failures are fundamentally concurrency control problems: agents concurrently read and write shared state, and long LLM inference windows amplify the risk of stale reads, lost updates, and inconsistent outcomes. Failure modes commonly attributed to coordination or communication breakdowns can be mapped directly onto classical concurrency anomalies.

evidence.title: Verified Detection and Prevention of Concurrency Anomalies in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Systems
evidence.quote: We model such sharing as long-running read-generate-write operations under deterministic-generation semantics -- the regime durable-execution engines enforce by deterministic replay -- and formalize four concurrency anomalies in TLA+: stale-generation, phantom-tool, causal-cascade, and tool-effect reordering, structural analogues of classical isolation anomalies, each with a TLC counter-example.

candidates.name: Authority-Preserving Memory Consolidation
candidates.summary: When consolidating interaction history into reusable long-term memory, persist an explicit authority label alongside each item — who asserted it and under what permission it may later be reused (user fact vs. attested observation vs. standing instruction) — and enforce that label at read and action time. Resolves the force that consolidation optimises for the claim and discards the qualifier: a summariser that faithfully preserves *what* was learned routinely drops *who was entitled to say it*, so a third-party remark or an unverified observation is later consumed as an authoritative standing instruction.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the arXiv-recency seam (August 2026). Original term: 'authority collapse'. Cross-product rather than cross-paper corroboration: the effect reproduces in 48 of 49 configurations spanning seven widely-used agent-memory systems and seven model backbones, which satisfies the 'recurring across products' bar within a single study. The mitigation is cheap and measured (labels restore 0.0% unauthorized actions with no task-success cost), which is what makes it pattern-shaped rather than merely a benchmark result.

evidence.title: When Memory Becomes Authority: Benchmarking Authority Collapse at the Memory Consolidation Boundary
evidence.quote: Yet consolidation also imposes an implicit authorization boundary: it determines whether stored information may later be consumed as a user fact, an attested observation, or a standing instruction.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. memory-poisoning is a write-time problem (untrusted surfaces write into memory with no provenance check); authority collapse occurs even when every write is benign and provenance-checked, because the consolidation step itself erases the source constraint. guardrail-erosion-through-compaction runs in the opposite direction — compaction paraphrases a hard safety rule into vague advice, weakening a constraint; here consolidation *strengthens* an ordinary claim into an instruction it was never licensed to be. memo-as-source-confusion is about staleness and failure to re-verify against artifacts, not about authorization level. deontic-token-delegation reifies obligations passed between agents along a delegation chain; this is a label attached to a memory item that must survive summarisation. provenance-ledger and lineage-tracking record what produced an output for audit; neither gates a memory read. [CURATOR NOTE: single unique scientific source — needs a second reference or an explicit single-source caveat before authoring.]

evidence.title: When Memory Becomes Authority: Benchmarking Authority Collapse at the Memory Consolidation Boundary
evidence.quote: We identify authority collapse, in which consolidation preserves a claim while erasing the source constraints governing its authorized use, causing the stored memory to imply greater authority than its source permits. [...] Across seven consolidators based on widely used agent-memory systems and seven LLM backbones, we observe authority collapse in 48 of 49 evaluated configurations. In a controlled action-grounded evaluation, collapsed memories without authority metadata yield a mean unauthorized-action rate of 50.3%. In an end-to-end evaluation, automatically predicted and persisted authority labels reduce the observed unauthorized-action rate from 16.9% to 0.0%, while benign task success remains essentially unchanged.

candidates.name: Adversarial Verifier Hardening Loop
candidates.summary: Harden the outcome verifier itself by running a three-role adversarial loop against it: a hacker agent tries to pass the verifier without solving the task, a fixer agent patches the verifier to reject each discovered exploit, and a solver agent confirms the patched verifier still admits legitimate solutions — iterating until attack success collapses, and transferring patches across tasks through a shared defense pool. Resolves the force that hand-written verifiers are brittle and that every patch reshapes what the verifier rewards (so hardening must iterate), while the solver role prevents over-tightening from silently rejecting correct work.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the arXiv-recency seam (June 2026, cs.AI/cs.SE). Original term: 'hacker-fixer loop'. The second reference supplies the general principle (verification must co-evolve with the generator; no fixed reward function survives capability growth), which is what lifts this from one benchmark-engineering trick to a recurring architectural force. Measured effect: attack success 62% to 0% on a held-out KernelBench exploit corpus, and a weaker model's loop successfully defends against strictly stronger attackers.

evidence.title: Hardening Agent Benchmarks with Adversarial Hacker-Fixer Loops
evidence.quote: The loop iterates: each patch reshapes what the verifier rewards, surfacing the next exploit. We further add verifier access, and let patches transfer across tasks, to broaden the exploits the loop discovers.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. verifier-aware-reward-hacking is the anti-pattern this pattern defends against — it names the failure (agent reads its grader and games it) but prescribes no hardening procedure. red-team-sandbox-reproduction re-runs a fixed suite of *already-known* alignment failures per release; here the adversary discovers novel exploits and the artifact being repaired is the grader, not the model or the prompt. evaluator-optimizer and generator-critic-separation loop a critic against a *candidate output*; this loop treats the evaluator as the thing under attack and requires a distinct third role (solver) purely as a false-rejection regression guard. eval-as-contract and eval-harness gate releases on an eval suite while remaining silent about the suite's own exploitability. process-reward-model trains a step-level verifier; it does not adversarially harden an outcome verifier.

evidence.title: Hardening Agent Benchmarks with Adversarial Hacker-Fixer Loops
evidence.quote: Agent benchmarks score submissions with outcome verifiers that are typically hand-written and brittle, leaving them open to reward hacking. We audit 1,968 tasks across five terminal-agent benchmarks and find 323 (16%) hackable by frontier models given only the task description. This corrupts both leaderboard rankings and RL training signal, yet the standard response is manual and reactive. We introduce the hacker-fixer loop, a method for building exploit-resistant verifiers without per-task manual patching. The loop alternates three LLM agents: a hacker tries to pass the verifier without solving the task, a fixer patches the verifier to reject each discovered exploit, and a solver confirms the patched verifier still admits legitimate solutions.

evidence.title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
evidence.quote: no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow; and verification must co-evolve with the generator

candidates.name: Memory Invalidation Contract
candidates.summary: Have the tool or service that taught the agent something attach a machine-readable validity contract to that lesson — a version stamp plus a cacheability hint at the granularity the data actually changes at — so the agent can evict exactly the cached learnings that a drift event invalidated and keep the rest, instead of re-deriving everything every episode or trusting a silently stale fix. Resolves the force that cross-episode caching of learned constraints and recovery procedures is where the token savings live, but server-side drift turns those cached lessons into silent failures, and the naive remedy (re-derive each episode) hands the savings straight back.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the arXiv-recency seam (arXiv 2609, submitted 31 Aug 2026). Original term: 'invalidation contract'. The granularity finding is the load-bearing liability for the pattern write-up: row-level invalidation raised first-try compliance by up to 66.7 points, while table-level invalidation destroyed co-located entries and dropped post-drift first-try rates to 0% on five of seven models — i.e. getting the invalidation granularity wrong is worse than not caching. The paper also documents a model-dependent 'compliance' axis (100% first-try on one model vs 11% on another, due to input-schema conservatism), which belongs in the pattern's consequences.

evidence.title: Invalidation Contracts for Cross-Episode Agent Memory
evidence.quote: Row-level invalidation raises compliance by 0 to 66.7 percentage points across the seven models, 55.6 to 66.7 on three, and recovers 29-33% of baseline token cost on four of seven models, while table-level invalidation destroys co-located entries and drops post-drift first-try rates to 0% on five of seven.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. reflexion writes cross-episode linguistic lessons from failures but has no validity protocol at all — it is precisely the practice this pattern instruments. tool-result-caching memoises deterministic tool *results* keyed by arguments within a session; this caches learned *procedural* knowledge (how to recover from a class of error) across episodes and gets its invalidation signal from the provider rather than from a TTL or argument key. cdc-vector-sync keeps a retrieval index in sync via a change-data-capture pipeline the consumer subscribes to; here the contract rides on the ordinary tool response and requires no separate event bus. adaptive-memory-decay ages items out by relevance/recency heuristics rather than by an authoritative validity stamp. silent-source-rot is the anti-pattern this prevents (an agent reports success while a wrapped external source has silently changed), stated from the failure side and without the protocol. [CURATOR NOTE: single unique scientific source — needs a second reference or an explicit single-source caveat before authoring.]

evidence.title: Invalidation Contracts for Cross-Episode Agent Memory
evidence.quote: LLM agents that cache recovery suggestions from API errors can skip re-derivation in later episodes, spending fewer tokens and fewer model calls on constraints they have already learned. Server-side data drift turns those cached fixes into silent failures, and the usual remedy, re-deriving on every episode, gives the savings back. We introduce invalidation contracts, a protocol layer that attaches version stamps and cacheability hints to every recovery suggestion so the client can evict stale entries without trial and error, and keep the rest.

candidates.name: Task-Pinned Model Routing
candidates.summary: Route once per task at admission and pin every subsequent LLM call in that workflow to the chosen backend, then update the routing policy from the task's terminal reward rather than from per-call signals. Resolves the force that agentic work is supervised only at task completion: a per-call router cannot attribute a delayed, task-level outcome back to any individual routing decision, so it optimises a signal it does not have — and pinning additionally makes the routing unit equal the supervision unit, which sidesteps explicit task-complexity estimation altogether.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the arXiv-recency seam (arXiv 2607, submitted 24 Jul 2026). Original term: 'task-consistent routing'. Reported effect: 7-8 accuracy points over latency-matched interpolation on tau2-Bench, and 7.1 points over the strongest single model on Terminal-Bench at 36% lower latency. Flagging honestly that this is one paper: the *force* (agentic routing is sequential and path-dependent with end-of-episode feedback) is separately argued in the budget-aware-routing literature, but the specific pin-at-admission remedy rests on this paper alone, so it is proposed at medium confidence.

evidence.title: TRACE-ROUTER: Task-Consistent and Adaptive Online Routing for Agentic AI
evidence.quote: By leveraging delayed task feedback, TRACE-Router learns routing policies that adapt to the workload while avoiding explicit task-complexity estimation.

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. multi-model-routing sends each *request* to the cheapest model that can handle it, and complexity-based-routing binds a request to a tier via an explicit difficulty classifier — this pattern routes at the granularity of a whole multi-call workflow and explicitly avoids complexity estimation, learning instead from the terminal reward. adaptive-compute-allocation varies thinking budget per query, not backend per task. bayesian-bandit-experimentation runs a bandit over agent/prompt *variants* to reallocate traffic for experimentation; here the bandit is the production router and its arm is the backend for one task. sla-aware-triage-scoring orders a work queue; it does not choose a model. open-weight-cascade and fallback-chain escalate across tiers mid-flight, which is exactly what pinning forbids. [CURATOR NOTE: single unique scientific source — needs a second reference or an explicit single-source caveat before authoring.]

evidence.title: TRACE-ROUTER: Task-Consistent and Adaptive Online Routing for Agentic AI
evidence.quote: Existing routers, primarily make independent routing decisions for each LLM call. However, agentic applications execute as long-horizon workflows whose quality is determined only by a delayed, task-level outcome. This mismatch prevents per-call routers from correctly attributing feedback to individual routing decisions. Towards mitigating this, we present TRACE-Router, a task-level routing framework that aligns routing with the unit of supervision. TRACE-Router assigns each task to a model once at admission using a contextual bandit, pins all subsequent LLM calls to the selected backend, and updates its policy using the task's terminal reward, jointly accounting for accuracy and latency.

raised_by.note: Cross-seam corroboration from the arxiv-listing scout. Two independent August 2026 papers supply the missing quantified force for pinning the backend for the life of a task. The Handoff Tax measures the penalty for switching mid-trajectory and adds a non-obvious asymmetry the pattern should record: the preferred interface reverses with direction — reducing the weak model's inherited trajectory improves escalation quality, while removing the strong model's trajectory degrades downshift. 'Beyond Tier Labels' independently establishes that a model's value is role- and deployment-conditioned rather than implied by its tier, which is the reason a per-call router mis-prices the substitution.

evidence.title: The Handoff Tax: Continuing Non-Native Trajectories in LLM Agents
evidence.quote: Across both model families, full-trajectory escalation recovers less than half of the LC-to-HC quality gap while incurring a substantial cost premium. We term this cost-quality penalty the handoff tax.

evidence.title: Beyond Tier Labels: Role- and Deployment-Dependent Model Substitution in Multi-Call LLM Workflows
evidence.quote: Large multi-call LLM systems pose a scientific problem that query-level routing does not capture: the value of a model depends on where it enters a dependent computation and on the deployment that surrounds that call.

candidates.name: Subgoal-Scoped Capability Closure
candidates.summary: Grant a capability for the subgoal that justified it, not for the run: compile the task contract into initial capabilities plus grant rules and explicit closure predicates, materialise each expansion as an opaque epoch-bound handle, remove the handle from the planner's interface the moment its closure predicate fires, and reject stale replay of a closed handle before any side effect executes. Resolves the force that agents are given whole-task tool permissions because permission changes are expensive to negotiate mid-run, leaving every capability live for the rest of the episode long after the subgoal it was granted for has closed.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the arXiv-recency seam (June/July 2026, cs.CR/cs.SE). Original term: 'lingering authority'; the reference implementation is named PORTICO (task contracts compiled into capabilities, grant rules, closure predicates and deny rules; a request-grant-invoke lifecycle over epoch-bound handles). The second reference is a systematization of 39 execution-security papers (2023-2026) that independently identifies the gap this pattern fills: benign out-of-scope agent actions at up to 17.1% are covered by no capability paper in its corpus. Reported effect in the primary paper: 10/10 post-closure capability reuse attempts rejected, against 10/10 permitted by a non-revoking control.

evidence.title: Lingering Authority: Revocable Resource-and-Effect Capabilities for Coding Agents
evidence.quote: even when a resource is needed only for one subgoal

raised_by.note: Scientific grounding. ephemeral-agent-identity mints and revokes an identity at *run* granularity — this pattern contracts authority *within* a run, at subgoal boundaries, which is where the exposure window actually lives. progressive-tool-access is the expansion half of the story (grant more as competency is proven) and has no closure or revocation mechanism; this is the contraction half, and the two compose. delegated-agent-authorization issues scoped short-lived credentials to an agent acting for a principal, but its scope is the delegation, not the subgoal, and it has no notion of a closure predicate or stale-handle replay rejection. tool-over-broad-scope is the adjacent anti-pattern but it is about *breadth* of a single tool's scope (one hallucinated argument escalates), not about *duration* of a correctly-scoped grant. tool-loadout and tool-loadout-hotswap concern which tools are visible for capability/context reasons, not authorization lifetime.

evidence.title: Lingering Authority: Revocable Resource-and-Effect Capabilities for Coding Agents
evidence.quote: a temporary resource/effect capability remains exposed after the episode that justified it has closed

evidence.title: The Balkanization of Execution-Security Research for AI Coding Agents: Isolation, Access Control, and Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use Vulnerabilities
evidence.quote: Benign but out-of-scope agent actions occurring at rates up to 17.1% under realistic prompting are addressed by no access-control or capability paper in the corpus.

candidates.name: Instruction Evolution (Evol-Instruct)
candidates.summary: Grow a training or eval instruction set by having the model itself rewrite each seed instruction into harder and broader variants along explicit evolution operators (add constraints, deepen, concretise, increase reasoning steps; and breadth-wise, mutate into a new but related task), then train on the evolved mixture. Resolves the force that human-authored instruction data is expensive and, worse, systematically under-samples the high-complexity tail that determines whether the resulting agent can follow multi-constraint instructions at all.

raised_by.note: Surfaced via the books-and-talks seam: it is a named chapter-level pattern (#16 of 32) in the O'Reilly 2026 book 'Generative AI Design Patterns' by Valliappa Lakshmanan and Hannes Hapke, in the chapter on extending model capabilities. Corroborated across three independent surfaces I opened: the book's Japanese edition TOC (原書名 'Generative AI Design Patterns', 発行日 2026年05月27日), the book's companion code repository, and the original WizardLM paper. Original Japanese term: 「パターン16：インストラクション進化」 (gloss: 'Pattern 16: Instruction Evolution').

evidence.title: 生成AIデザインパターン ―AIエージェント構築、アプリケーション開発のベストプラクティス (O'Reilly Japan)
evidence.quote: 5.5　パターン16：インストラクション進化

evidence.title: lakshmanok/generative-ai-design-patterns — companion code for the O'Reilly book
